paragraphs.heading: Where the crust ends
paragraphs.text: The Mohorovičić discontinuity, usually just called the Moho, is the boundary between Earth's crust and its mantle. It is named after the Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovičić. It separates both oceanic and continental crust from the mantle below and marks a change in what the rock is made of. Scientists locate it by a clear change in the speed of seismic waves as they pass through rock of different density.

paragraphs.heading: How deep it lies
paragraphs.text: The Moho is 5 to 10 km beneath the ocean floor and 20 to 90 km beneath typical continents, about 35 km on average. It lies almost entirely inside the lithosphere, the hard outer layer of Earth that includes the crust. Only under mid-ocean ridges does it match the lithosphere–asthenosphere boundary, which is the depth where mantle rock turns noticeably ductile.

paragraphs.heading: A jump in wave speed
paragraphs.text: Just above the Moho, P-waves, the primary seismic waves, travel at speeds typical of basalt, 6.7 to 7.2 km/s. Just below, they move at speeds like those in peridotite or dunite, 7.6 to 8.6 km/s. This rise of about 1 km/s signals a real change in material, and it is widely taken as the bottom of the crust. The change happens across a transition zone up to 500 meters thick.

paragraphs.heading: An earthquake near Zagreb
paragraphs.text: In 1909 Mohorovičić was studying records of a local earthquake in Zagreb. He saw two separate sets of P-waves and S-waves spreading from its focus. He knew that earthquake waves travel at speeds proportional to the density of the rock carrying them. So he reasoned that the second set could only come from a sharp change in density within the Earth, and he worked out its depth as about 54 km.

paragraphs.heading: Not always a simple line
paragraphs.text: From the 1980s geologists realized the Moho does not always match the crust-mantle boundary defined by rock makeup. Xenoliths, pieces of lower crust and upper mantle rock carried up by volcanic eruptions, helped show this. Away from continental cratons, the change from crust to mantle can be up to 20 km thick and is laced with basaltic intrusions. So seismic data alone must be read with care. Ancient Moho zones can also be seen above ground in ophiolites around the world.

paragraphs.heading: Trying to drill there
paragraphs.text: In the early 1960s Project Mohole set out to drill to the Moho from the deep ocean, but it was cancelled in 1966 after opposition, mismanagement and cost overruns. Soviet scientists drilled the Kola Superdeep Borehole from 1970 to 1992, reaching 12,260 meters, the world's deepest hole, before giving up. From late 2015 the drill-ship JOIDES Resolution aimed for 1.5 km at Atlantis Bank in the Indian Ocean but did not even reach 1.3 km. Reaching the Moho by drilling is still an important goal.
